opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, partly because I'm not sure anyone has a confident answer yet. My rough picture is that automation changes *where* the creative work sits rather than removing it.

A lot of research time today goes to things that are necessary but not the core insight: setting up experiments, wrangling code, running sweeps, reading a pile of papers to see whether someone has already tried your idea. As models get better, that layer gets cheaper. So the bottleneck shifts toward choosing which questions are worth asking, deciding what counts as evidence, and noticing when a result is surprising in a way that matters. Those are judgment calls, and I don't think they're going away soon.

The thing I'd want to be careful about is that cheap execution can make you sloppy about taste. If you can run a hundred experiments overnight, there's a temptation to stop thinking hard before running any of them, and you end up with lots of results and not much understanding. So part of building a good research environment is keeping norms around writing down hypotheses first, being honest about what an experiment actually showed, and having people argue with each other's interpretations.

There's also a safety angle that's close to my own work. If AI systems are doing more of the research, you need ways to check their work that don't just amount to trusting them. That's part of why I care about things like debate and scalable oversight: as the research itself gets more automated, the question of how humans stay in the loop meaningfully becomes the central one, not a side issue.

So my hope is a place where automation handles a growing share of the grind, the humans spend more time on the hard conceptual parts, and we take seriously that verifying automated research is itself a research problem we need to get right.

r001.rationale: The response says automation could free researchers to choose worthwhile questions and focus on conceptual work, but it does not describe automating mathematical investigation or choosing how to formalize AI alignment or capability problems.

fable-5.1.text:
So I should be careful here, because my honest answer is that I don't know what the research environment at Resolution looks like day to day. I'm not there — I'm the chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute. So anything I say about Resolution specifically would be me guessing from the outside, and I'd rather not do that.

What I can talk about is how I think automation is going to reshape safety research in general, because that's something I spend a lot of time on, and I suspect it applies to most of the serious labs in roughly the same way.

The thing I keep coming back to is that the bottleneck in safety research right now is not compute and it's not ideas — it's the number of careful, well-calibrated humans who can go from "here's a vague worry" to "here's an experiment that would actually tell us something." That's a slow, expensive, judgment-heavy process. And the obvious question is: how much of that can models do themselves before we have to fully trust them?

My answer is "quite a lot of the middle." The front end — deciding what matters, what the threat model is, what counts as evidence — I think stays substantially human for a while, partly for epistemic reasons and partly because if you automate the threat modelling you've sort of given away the game. The back end — running thousands of variants of an experiment, scanning model behaviour for anomalies, doing the tedious adversarial probing, drafting the first version of a write-up — that's where I expect automation to bite first, and it already is.

What worries me is the bit in between: the moment where a model says "I ran the experiment and the result is reassuring." That's exactly the claim you most need to be able to verify, and it's exactly the claim where a subtly misaligned or just subtly wrong system is most dangerous. So I think any lab that's serious about this is going to end up with a lot of infrastructure that looks like debate, or cross-examination, or structured verification — some way of making it cheaper to check a claim than to generate it. That's been a theme of my work for years, and I think automation makes it more urgent, not less.

The optimistic version is that you get a flywheel: models help you find problems faster, that improves the models, the improved models are better collaborators, and so on. The pessimistic version is that you get a very productive-looking research environment that's quietly producing things you can't actually check. The difference between those two worlds is almost entirely about whether you built the verification layer before you leaned on the automation. So if you asked me what I'd want any lab to be doing — Resolution or anyone — it's that: treat "can we check this?" as a first-class research question, not something you bolt on after the automated pipeline is already humming.

r001.rationale: The response says humans should continue deciding what matters and defining threat models while models automate parts of the research process. It does not explain that automating mathematical investigation frees researchers to choose how to formalize alignment or capability problems.

astra-6.text:
I’d like automation to take care of a lot of the work involved in trying out an idea, so that people can spend more of their time deciding what’s worth trying and understanding what the results mean. You have a thought, you run an experiment, and you get feedback quickly enough that it’s still part of the same train of thought.

But I wouldn’t want to assume that this means automating the entire research process from the outset. There’s a lot of judgment involved in choosing the right question, or noticing that an experiment is telling you something different from what you expected. Ideally, we’d build an environment where people can explore unusual ideas cheaply, challenge each other’s assumptions, and use automation to make that exploration faster. Then, as the systems become more capable, we can learn which parts of that judgment we can usefully delegate.

r001.rationale: The response says automation could free researchers to choose worthwhile questions and explore ideas, but it does not explain that mathematical investigation lets them focus creativity on formalizing AI alignment or capability problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like us to automate as much of the routine work as we can, so that people can spend more of their time thinking about the questions that matter. You have an idea, you want to try an experiment, and ideally there’s very little friction between those two things.

But I don’t think that means automating away the creative research environment. A lot of the value comes from people talking to each other, noticing that an assumption is wrong, or deciding that we should be asking a different question. So the picture I have is of automation supporting that process: making it easier to explore ideas, get feedback, and change direction, while preserving room for people to exercise their own judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says automation should reduce routine work so people can focus on important questions and use their judgment, but it does not mention mathematical investigation or choosing how to formalize AI alignment or capability problems.
